key_decisions: Alice's arc is written as deference -> self-possession (arc-alice-authority/identity). Her facade (polite surface / sharp, fair true self) must crack in steps: ch007 walk-out, ch008 'Nonsense!', ch009 'I've a right to think', ch012 'Who cares for you?'.

The dream figures are read as adult-authority traits: Queen = capricious, toothless adult temper (also Alice's own self-scolding: she boxes her own ears at croquet, ch001-p24); King = pompous procedural authority that gives way; Duchess = moralising, rough nursery adult; White Rabbit = tyranny of the clock and of rank; Hatter = adult making personal remarks, tied to tea-time; March Hare = etiquette hypocrisy; Dormouse = drowsy storyteller who scolds a child for 'growing'; Cheshire Cat (Dinah echo) = the one equal, a model of self-possession.
The Queen's menace must feel real until the ch009 reveal (Gryphon aside ch009-p46 and King's pardon ch009-p42). Screenplay must not undercut it earlier.
The sister is given a no-dialogue, no-intervention taboo at the trial glimpse, so that Alice, not an adult, ends the dream.

consistency_flags_for_logic_qa.issue: Reportedly boxed the Queen's ears (ch008-p40) yet cannot speak up to her face (ch009-p31-p33). This is in the source and unresolved there. Suggested reading: a flash of kitchen temper that put her under sentence, now followed by fear. Not patched.

Secret pardoner (ch009-p42) versus eager fetcher of the executioner (ch008-p60) and threatener of the Hatter (ch011-p27). Resolved in character as self-protection; flagged so it is not read as a contradiction.

The inkstand thrown at Bill (ch012-p55) sits uneasily with SUP-014's no-contact rule. This is a staging question, not a personality one: the inkstand should land on the slate/desk, and ink splash only.
